title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(g) Pass-Through Entities
description: 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) limits how partners, S corporation shareholders and other owners use passed-through R&D credits.
summary: Section 41(g) of 26 U.S.C. limits how partners, S corporation shareholders, sole proprietors, and trust or estate beneficiaries use passed-through R&D tax credits in the United States. The credit can offset only the tax attributable to income from the specific research-performing business; excess credits carry over, remaining ring-fenced to that entity, with California applying parallel rules.

body.text: Section 41(g) of 26 U.S.C. limits how partners, S corporation shareholders, sole proprietors, and trust or estate beneficiaries use passed-through R&D tax credits in the United States. The credit can offset only the tax attributable to income from the specific research-performing business; excess credits carry over, remaining ring-fenced to that entity, with California applying parallel rules.
Executive Summary and Statutory Purpose of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(g), codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) under the statutory heading "Special rule for pass-thru of credit," establishes a mandatory statutory ring-fence governing the utilization of the Credit for Increasing Research Activities when qualified research expenses (QREs) are incurred by pass-through entities and unincorporated businesses. Whereas the research and development (R&D) tax credit determined under IRC § 41(a) generally operates as a component of the general business credit under IRC § 38—subject to the overarching net income tax liability ceiling of IRC § 38(c)—Section 41(g) imposes an additional, entity-specific limitation on individual owners, partners, S corporation shareholders, and trust or estate beneficiaries. Specifically, the plain text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) restricts the amount of passed-through research credit a taxpayer may claim in any taxable year to an amount—separately computed with respect to such person's interest in the specific trade, business, or entity—equal to the amount of tax attributable to that portion of the person's taxable income which is allocable or apportionable to the person's interest in such trade, business, or entity.

The structural function of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) is to prevent the syndication and commoditization of R&D tax credits as cross-income tax shelters. When research expenditures are incurred by partnerships, limited liability companies (LLCs) taxed as partnerships, S corporations, estates, trusts, or sole proprietorships, the resulting tax credits flow through to the underlying taxpayers (computed on Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities) and are reported on Form 1040. In the absence of Section 41(g), an individual taxpayer with substantial unrelated W-2 wage compensation, portfolio dividends, or capital gains could acquire a passive or non-operating equity stake in a research-intensive pass-through entity and apply the passed-through credits to offset tax liabilities derived from entirely unrelated economic sources. By confining credit absorption strictly to the tax liability generated by the R&D-performing business unit, Section 41(g) aligns the realization of the tax subsidy with the commercial profitability of the underlying research venture.
Legislative Origins and Evolution of the Pass-Through Limitation

The statutory architecture of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) traces directly to the initial enactment of the federal research credit in Section 221 of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA), Pub. L. 97-34, 95 Stat. 172, 241–247 (1981). Confronted with declining domestic private-sector research expenditures during the late 1970s and early 1980s relative to major industrial competitors such as West Germany and Japan, and recognizing the reluctance of ongoing businesses to bear the substantial staffing, supply, and equipment costs required to initiate or expand research programs, Congress introduced a nonrefundable incremental tax credit codified under former IRC § 44F to incentivize marginal increases in qualified research spending paid or incurred after June 30, 1981.

As documented by the Joint Committee on Taxation in its General Explanation of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (commonly termed the "Blue Book"), lawmakers sought to ensure that the newly enacted subsidy rewarded genuine operating investment rather than facilitating personal tax shelter arrangements. Accordingly, Congress embedded explicit pass-through utilization restrictions within original IRC § 44F(g). Through subsequent legislative restructurings of the Internal Revenue Code—first the redesignation of IRC § 44F as IRC § 30 under the Tax Reform Act of 1984 (Pub. L. 98-369, §§ 474(i)(1)(B) and 612(e)(1)), and subsequently its permanent redesignation as IRC § 41 under Section 231 of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. 99-514, § 231(d)(3)(C)(ii))—Congress preserved and fortified the subsection (g) limitation.

During the 1986 tax reform deliberations (reflected in H.R. Rep. No. 99-426 and S. Rep. No. 99-313), Congress and the Joint Committee on Taxation reiterated that unchecked flow-through incentives distorted capital allocation by inducing high-income individuals to concentrate capital in tax-favored vehicles purely for tax reduction. In Section 231(d)(3)(C)(ii) of the Tax Reform Act of 1986, Congress amended IRC § 41(g) generally to dedicate subsection (g) specifically to the "Special rule for pass-thru of credit," while relocating the general tax liability limitation to IRC § 38(c). Subsequently, in Section 1002(h)(1) of the Technical and Miscellaneous Revenue Act of 1988 (TAMRA, Pub. L. 100-647), Congress inserted the final sentence of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g), explicitly codifying the rule that any research credit exceeding the subsection (g) pass-through limitation may be carried to other taxable years under IRC § 39, provided that the subsection (g) limitation is applied in lieu of the general IRC § 38(c) limitation in every carryover year. By tethering the usability of the research credit to the specific income stream of the credit-generating entity and prohibiting the credit from reducing tax liability below zero or offsetting unrelated aggregate income, Congress established a durable structural boundary that remains in force under current law.
Federal Statutory Mechanics and Entity Apportionment Rules
Covered Claimants and Statutory Apportionment Directives

The plain text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)(1)–(4) delineates four distinct categories of pass-through and unincorporated claimants subject to the separate tax-attributable ceiling: (1) an individual who owns an interest in an unincorporated trade or business (including a sole proprietorship reported on Schedule C or a single-member LLC treated as a disregarded entity for federal tax purposes) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)(1); (2) a partner in a partnership (including a member of a multi-member LLC classified as a partnership for federal tax purposes) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)(2); (3) a beneficiary of an estate or trust under 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)(3); and (4) a shareholder in an S corporation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(g)(4). Before the individual-level tax-attributable cap is computed on Form 1040, the statute and accompanying Treasury Regulations under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(a) prescribe distinct entity-level allocation rules depending on the legal classification of the pass-through vehicle.

cells: S Corporation
Pro-rata allocation among shareholders on a strict per-share, per-day basis.
Special allocations are prohibited; credit distribution must mirror stock ownership percentages throughout the taxable year.
Partnership / Multi-Member LLC
Computed at the partnership level and allocated in accordance with IRC § 704 and the proportion of IRC § 174 / § 174A expenditures.
Credit allocation cannot be decoupled from the economic burden of the underlying research and experimental costs.
Estate or Trust
Apportioned between the fiduciary entity and the beneficiaries based on the entity income allocable to each.
Follows trust or estate distributable net income allocation ratios between retained fiduciary income and beneficiary distributions.
Unincorporated Trade or Business / Disregarded Entity
Retained 100% by the individual proprietor or single-member owner.
Credit utilization is strictly segregated and capped by the net taxable income generated specifically by that trade or business.

body.text: For S corporations, IRC §§ 1366 and 1377 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(1)(i) mandate that for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1982, the research credit computed for the corporation be apportioned pro-rata among shareholders on a per-share, per-day basis, precluding any disproportionate or special assignment of credits to specific shareholders. For estates and trusts, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(2) directs that the research credit computed for the estate or trust for any taxable year be apportioned among the fiduciary entity and its beneficiaries in direct proportion to the estate or trust income allocable to each party. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(4), any credit amount apportioned to a shareholder, beneficiary, or partner must be taken into account in the taxable year of such person within which the taxable year of the corporation, estate, trust, or partnership ends.

Partnership allocations are governed by a rigorous economic substance standard under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(a)(3)(i). When a partnership incurs QREs in carrying on a trade or business, the credit is determined at the partnership level and allocated to partners in accordance with IRC § 704 and the regulations thereunder, specifically cross-referencing Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b)(4)(ii). Because the research credit is an expenditure-based credit rather than an income-based credit, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(3)(i) explicitly mandates that the credit be allocated among the partners in the exact same proportion as the partnership's underlying section 174 research and experimental expenditures are allocated for the taxable year. Consequently, a partnership cannot allocate 100% of its R&D tax credits to a high-tax investor unless that investor also validly bears 100% of the economic cost of the underlying research and experimental expenditures with substantial economic effect reflected in the partnership capital accounts under IRC § 704(b). A narrow exception exists under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(3)(ii) for certain joint venture research expenditures to which Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(4)(ii) applies: those expenses are treated as paid or incurred directly by the partners rather than by the partnership, meaning each partner aggregates its distributive share of those expenses with its own research expenses to compute the credit directly at the partner level, and the pass-through limitation of IRC § 41(g) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(c) does not apply to that partner-computed credit.
Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7 and the § 1.53-3 Fractional Formula

The operational calculation of the 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) ceiling is governed by Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(c) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-7(c)), which directs that the special rule contained in Section 41(g) for the pass-through of the credit in the case of an individual who owns an interest in an unincorporated trade or business, is a partner in a partnership, is a beneficiary of an estate or trust, or is a shareholder in an S corporation must be applied in accordance with the mathematical principles set forth in Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3 (26 C.F.R. § 1.53-3). Under the fractional methodology of Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c), the maximum research credit allowable to a pass-through owner for a given taxable year is isolated using the following proportional formula:

In this formulation, the "Total Net Tax Liability" multiplied by the fraction corresponds to the taxpayer's net income tax limitation for the taxable year computed under IRC § 38(c) (substituting for the legacy IRC § 53(a) limitation referenced in the historical text of 26 C.F.R. § 1.53-3(c)). The numerator of the fraction represents the portion of the taxpayer's net taxable income for the taxable year that is directly allocable or apportionable to the taxpayer's interest in the specific R&D-generating entity. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(d)(1)–(3), the portion of a taxpayer's taxable income attributable to an interest in a partnership, estate or trust, or S corporation is computed by taking the amount of gross income from that entity that the taxpayer is required to include in gross income (including, as illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(d)(4), Example 2, partnership distributive share of ordinary income and guaranteed payments, or S corporation pass-through income and shareholder salary in Example 1) and reducing it by: (i) the deductions allowed to the taxpayer that are directly attributable to the taxpayer's interest in the entity, and (ii) a proportionate share of the taxpayer's deductions that are not attributable to any specific activity (as defined in Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(e), such as itemized personal deductions or the standard deduction). The denominator of the fraction under Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) represents the taxpayer's aggregate taxable income from all sources for the taxable year (historically adjusted by the pre-1987 zero-bracket amount referenced in legacy Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c), which is obsolete in modern Form 1040 computations where the standard deduction or itemized deductions are already subtracted to arrive at taxable income).

This fractional mechanism creates an absolute cliff when a research-performing pass-through entity operates at a tax loss. Early-stage technology, biotechnology, and engineering partnerships or S corporations frequently incur substantial QREs before achieving commercial profitability, resulting in an ordinary business loss on the owner's Schedule K-1. When the entity reports zero taxable income or a net loss, the numerator of the Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) fraction is zero. Because a zero numerator reduces the entire fraction (0 divided by Total Taxable Income) to 0, the taxpayer's Section 41(g) tax-attributable limit for that entity is $0, barring the taxpayer from claiming any portion of the passed-through R&D credit in the current year regardless of how much tax the taxpayer owes on unrelated W-2 salaries, investment income, or profitable interests in other businesses.
Methodological Conflict: Pro-Rata Fraction vs. Marginal Rate Computation

A major technical dispute in federal and state tax controversy involves the tension between the regulatory pro-rata fractional method and the practitioner-developed marginal rate method for computing the "tax attributable" under Section 41(g). Because the U.S. individual income tax schedule (as well as state counterparts such as California's Personal Income Tax) imposes progressive marginal tax brackets, the effective tax rate on a taxpayer's aggregate taxable income is lower than the statutory rate applied to the highest marginal dollar earned.

cells: Computational Logic
Multiplies total net tax liability by the ratio of entity taxable income to total taxable income.
Treats pass-through income (e.g., Schedule K-1 Box 1) as the topmost layer of aggregate taxable income.
Effective Tax Rate Applied
Applies the taxpayer's blended average effective tax rate across all progressive brackets.
Applies the taxpayer's highest statutory marginal tax bracket(s) to the pass-through income stream.
Impact on § 41(g) Ceiling
Produces a lower tax-attributable ceiling, forcing more credit into carryforward status.
Maximizes the current-year tax-attributable ceiling, accelerating current-year credit utilization.
Regulatory & Audit Posture
Directly supported by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-7(c) and § 1.53-3(c); enforced by IRS and FTB examiners upon audit.
Lacks explicit regulatory authorization for partnership/S corp § 41(g) claims; faces high risk of examination adjustment and disallowance.

body.text: Under the marginal rate ("with and without") approach—often promoted in commercial practitioner literature—practitioners compute the taxpayer's total tax liability with the pass-through income included and subtract the hypothetical tax liability computed without the pass-through income, effectively stacking the Schedule K-1 ordinary business income at the very top of the progressive rate schedule. While intuitive as a "but-for" measure of incremental tax caused by the entity (and notably adopted by the California Franchise Tax Board in the specific context of single-member LLC disregarded entities on Form FTB 3523 instructions), the marginal rate method lacks federal regulatory sanction for partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(c), which explicitly mandates applying the proportional ratio of Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c). Because the pro-rata method blends lower and higher tax brackets into an average effective rate and further reduces the numerator by a proportionate share of non-business deductions under Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(d)(1)(ii), it yields a substantially lower current-year utilization ceiling. Upon examination, Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agents routinely reject marginal rate computations in favor of the strict Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3 fraction, exposing aggressive claimants to deficiency assessments and recomputed carryforward schedules.
Dynamic Interaction with IRC Section 280C(c) Elections

The ceiling imposed by 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) does not operate in isolation; its mathematical numerator is directly altered by the mandatory coordination rules of IRC § 280C(c). Enacted in 1988 (Pub. L. 100-647) to prevent taxpayers from claiming both a full deduction (or capital account charge) for research expenditures and a full tax credit under IRC § 41 for the exact same dollar of research expenditure, Section 280C(c) presents pass-through entities with two mutually exclusive computational paths. Across three distinct statutory eras, Congress has adjusted the statutory mechanics of IRC § 280C(c) while preserving this fundamental trade-off. For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022, former IRC § 280C(c)(1) required taxpayers claiming the full IRC § 41(a) credit to reduce their current IRC § 174 deduction by the full amount of the research credit, unless they made a timely election on an original return under former IRC § 280C(c)(3) to claim a reduced credit. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) mandated 5-year amortization of domestic research and experimental expenditures (and 15-year amortization of foreign expenditures) under IRC § 174, redesignated the reduced credit election from § 280C(c)(3) to § 280C(c)(2), and modified § 280C(c)(1) so that a capital account reduction was required only if the § 41(a)(1) credit exceeded the current-year deductible research expense. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302, enacted July 4, 2025) enacted new IRC § 174A to restore immediate deductibility (or elective 60-month amortization under § 174A(c)) for domestic research or experimental expenditures, while amending 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) generally to restore the full dollar-for-dollar deduction reduction.

Under current 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(b)(2)(B)), the domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in IRC § 174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to capital account must be reduced by 100% of the gross research credit allowed under IRC § 41(a) (effectuated via an add-back to ordinary business income on Schedule M-1 or M-3 of the entity return). Alternatively, under the reduced credit election of 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(2) (historically codified at IRC § 280C(c)(3) prior to the TCJA redesignation), the entity elects on Form 6765 on a timely filed original return (including extensions) to claim a statutorily reduced research credit—reduced by the product of the gross credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under IRC § 11(b), which is 21%, yielding a credit equal to 79% of the gross credit—thereby preserving 100% of its allowable IRC § 174A / § 174 deduction in the current year. Once made for a taxable year, the § 280C(c)(2) election is irrevocable and ordinarily cannot be made on an amended return—subject only to the one-time statutory exception under the OBBBA and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (issued August 28, 2025), which permitted eligible small businesses meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test ($31 million or less in average annual gross receipts for 2022–2024) that elected retroactive § 174A domestic R&E expensing for 2022–2024 to make a late § 280C(c)(2) election or revoke a prior election on an amended return or administrative adjustment request filed by the earlier of July 6, 2026, or the expiration of the IRC § 6511 refund statute of limitations.

For a pass-through entity and its owners, the Section 280C(c) choice triggers a second-order feedback loop within the Section 41(g) fractional formula. If the pass-through entity foregoes the reduced credit election under § 280C(c)(2) and instead applies the standard deduction reduction rule of § 280C(c)(1), its operating deductions are reduced by the amount of the gross credit. That reduction in entity-level deductions mathematically increases the entity's net ordinary business income. When this higher net taxable income flows through to the owner's Schedule K-1, it directly increases the numerator of the Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) fraction, thereby expanding the owner's Section 41(g) tax-attributable limit. Conversely, electing the 79% reduced credit under § 280C(c)(2) preserves the full research deduction, which lowers entity-level net taxable income and compresses the owner's Section 41(g) utilization ceiling.

Analysis of this mechanism reveals a critical multi-year modeling trade-off: if an entity operates in a deep net loss position such that even after adding back the gross credit under § 280C(c)(1) the entity remains in a net tax loss, the owner's Section 41(g) numerator remains zero while the owner is simultaneously deprived of current research deductions. Furthermore, the Internal Revenue Manual (IRM Part 8.7.1, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, IRC 41) explicitly directs IRS Appeals Technical Employees (ATEs) to verify that taxpayers not making a valid reduced credit election on an original timely filed return under IRC § 280C(c) have demonstrably reduced their underlying research deductions regardless of whether the credit can be utilized in the current computation year, and to enforce the IRC § 38(c), § 39, and § 41(g) limitations strictly on the resulting pass-through credit.
Carryback and Carryforward Substitution Rules Under IRC Section 39

When a pass-through owner's allocable research credit exceeds the Section 41(g) ceiling in a taxable year, the excess credit is not forfeited; instead, it enters the general business credit carryover regime of IRC § 39, which provides a 1-year carryback period and a 20-year carryforward period. To prevent the carryforward mechanism from circumventing the pass-through ring-fence in future years, the final sentence of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) (enacted by TAMRA, Pub. L. 100-647, § 1002(h)(1)) establishes a strict statutory substitution rule. Specifically, when applying the carryover provisions of IRC § 39, the separate Section 41(g) tax-attributable limitation must be substituted in lieu of the general business credit limitation of IRC § 38(c).

cells: Carryback Period
1 Year (IRC § 39)
Permits retroactive offset against prior-year tax liability, strictly capped by that prior year's § 41(g) limit for the same entity.
Carryforward Period
20 Years (IRC § 39)
Provides a 20-year horizon for pre-profit startup entities to generate positive taxable income and absorb suspended credits.
Limitation Substitution
IRC § 41(g) replaces IRC § 38(c)
Forces the carryforward to remain perpetually ring-fenced to the specific generating entity's income stream across all carryover years.
Entity Transformation
Permitted under Treas. Reg. §§ 1.41-7(d) and 1.53-3(f)
Unused carryforwards survive changes in business form (e.g., partnership incorporating or S election terminating) when tested against successor income.

body.text: Consequently, the excess R&D credit remains tethered to the specific trade, business, or entity that generated it across the entire 1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward horizon. In every subsequent carryover year, the taxpayer must recompute the Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) fraction for that specific entity and may absorb the carried-forward credit only to the extent of current-year tax attributable to taxable income from that exact entity. At the same time, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(d) and Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(f) provide a vital continuity safeguard: a taxpayer to whom a research credit has been passed through is not barred from applying the unused carryover in a subsequent carryback or carryover year merely because the entity that earned the credit changes its legal form of conducting business (such as a partnership incorporating into a C or S corporation, or an S corporation terminating its subchapter S election and paying taxable dividends as a C corporation), provided the nature of its trade or business essentially remains the same and the carryforward continues to be tested against the income attributable to the taxpayer's interest in the successor entity in its revised form.
California R&D Tax Credit Conformity and Pass-Through Divergence
Statutory Architecture Under R&TC Sections 23609 and 17052.12

The State of California administers a parallel R&D tax credit regime codified under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (under Part 11, the Corporation Tax Law, or CTL) and R&TC § 17052.12 (under Part 10, the Personal Income Tax Law, or PITL). While both California statutes incorporate the foundational framework of IRC § 41 by reference, California imposes significant statutory modifications that alter both the calculation of the credit and its longitudinal utilization by pass-through entities.

First, under R&TC § 23609(c)(2) and § 17052.12(d), California enforces strict geographic ring-fencing, limiting "qualified research" and "basic research" exclusively to activities conducted within the geographic borders of California and requiring multi-state businesses to include only gross receipts from the sale of property delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California and to exclude out-of-state expenditures. Second, California applies modified credit rates and methodologies: for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2000, R&TC § 23609(b)(3) and § 17052.12(b)(3) modify the federal 20% rate in IRC § 41(a)(1) to allow a 15% credit on excess QREs over base-period research expenses, while R&TC § 23609(b)(3)(B) modifies IRC § 41(a)(2) to allow a 24% credit on basic research payments for C corporations (whereas basic research payments under IRC § 41(a)(2) are disapplied under R&TC § 17052.12(c) for personal income tax filers and are unavailable to S corporations under IRC § 41(e)(7)(E)). Moreover, California explicitly declines to conform to the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(5) and retains instead a modified three-tier Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC) under IRC § 41(c)(4) with reduced statutory tier rates of 1.49%, 1.98%, and 2.48%.

Third, unlike the federal 1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward window under IRC § 39, California R&D credits cannot be carried back, are non-refundable, and do not expire; under R&TC § 23609(f) and § 17052.12(e), excess California credits carry forward indefinitely to succeeding taxable years until exhausted. Crucially, R&TC § 23609(j) (redesignated as subdivision (k) in subsequent legislative amendments) and R&TC § 17052.12(i) (redesignated as subdivision (j) in Senate Bill 711, Stats. 2025, Ch. 231) explicitly conform to IRC § 41(g) with a state-specific structural modification: (1) the last sentence of IRC § 41(g) (which references federal IRC §§ 39 and 38(c)) does not apply, and (2) if the research credit determined under IRC § 41(a) for any taxable year exceeds the limitation of IRC § 41(g), that excess amount is carried over to subsequent taxable years under the indefinite carryover rules of R&TC § 23609(f) or § 17052.12(e), except that the limitation of IRC § 41(g) must be taken into account in each subsequent carryover year.
The California S Corporation "1/3 Rule" Dual-Track Mechanism

The sharpest divergence between federal and California pass-through R&D credit mechanics occurs in the treatment of S corporations. Unlike the federal system—where S corporations generally pay no entity-level income tax—California imposes a mandatory 1.5% entity-level franchise or income tax on an S corporation's net income (or 3.5% for financial S corporations), subject to an $800 annual minimum franchise tax. To manage state fiscal exposure while maintaining pass-through incentives, R&TC § 23803 and California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) procedures (codified in Chapter 12 of the FTB S Corporation Manual and Form FTB 3523 Instructions) enforce a dual-track regime known as the "1/3 Rule".

Because the California R&D credit is allowed under both the Corporation Tax Law (R&TC § 23609) and the Personal Income Tax Law (R&TC § 17052.12), separate credit computations and utilization rules apply at the corporate and shareholder levels. At the corporate entity level, under R&TC § 23803(a)(1), an S corporation computes its California R&D credit at 100% on Form FTB 3523 using Corporation Tax Law rules, but may apply only one-third (1/3) of its computed credit (transferred to Schedule C of Form 100S) to offset its 1.5% (or 3.5%) entity-level tax liability down to, but not below, the $800 minimum franchise tax. The remaining two-thirds (2/3) of the credit at the corporate level is permanently disregarded and extinguished; it cannot be utilized by the S corporation or carried forward at the corporate level to offset future entity-level franchise taxes. Any unused portion of the allowable 1/3 corporate credit exceeding the current-year entity tax above the minimum franchise tax may be carried forward indefinitely at the S corporation level, though if the S corporation subsequently revokes or terminates its S election and converts to a C corporation, the unused 1/3 credit is suspended during C corporation years.

At the shareholder personal income tax level, however, the S corporation is statutorily permitted to pass through 100% of the unreduced computed California R&D credit (calculated under Personal Income Tax Law rules) pro-rata to its shareholders on Schedule K-1 (100S). Once reported on the shareholder's individual California return, the full 100% passed-through credit is governed by IRC § 41(g) (via R&TC § 17052.12), restricting current-year absorption strictly to the shareholder's California Personal Income Tax (PIT) liability attributable to their proportionate share of the S corporation's net income. Conversely, if a C corporation possesses unused California R&D credit carryforwards prior to electing S corporation status, California modifies IRC § 1371(b)(1) via R&TC § 23803: those legacy C corporation carryforwards are reduced to one-third (1/3) upon conversion (with the remaining 2/3 permanently disregarded) to offset future 1.5% entity-level S corporation tax, and are permanently barred from passing through to the S corporation's shareholders. Furthermore, with respect to the IRC § 280C(c) and R&TC § 24440 expense reduction rules, if an S corporation does not elect the reduced credit on a timely filed original California return, it must report an add-back under "Other Additions" on Form 100S equal to the 1/3 corporate-level credit while making a full 100% credit add-back adjustment on Schedule K to ordinary business income for the shareholder pass-through computation (and taxpayers may make different IRC § 280C(c) elections for California and federal purposes).
Partnership Allocations under IRC § 704(b) and Executive Credit Caps

For California partnerships (filing Form 565) and multi-member LLCs taxed as partnerships (filing Form 568), the FTB enforces federal IRC § 704(b) economic substance principles alongside R&TC § 17039(e). Because R&D credits are non-deductible items that do not directly reduce a partner's capital account, special allocations of the California R&D credit are respected on audit only if the written partnership operating agreement allocates the credit in the exact proportion that the partners bore the economic burden of the underlying QREs, and those expenditure allocations possess substantial economic effect in the partnership capital accounts under IRC § 704(b) and Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b)(4)(ii).

At the administrative and legislative level, California pass-through claimants must also navigate periodic statutory caps on credit utilization enacted to manage state budget volatility. Pursuant to California Senate Bill 167 and Senate Bill 175 (Chapter 42, Statutes of 2024, codified at R&TC §§ 17039.4 and 23036.4), for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, California law imposes an aggregate $5,000,000 annual cap on business credit utilization—encompassing the R&D credit and all prior-year carryforwards—per taxpayer (or in the aggregate across a combined reporting group), following an earlier $5,000,000 credit limitation and net operating loss (NOL) suspension enacted for 2020 through 2022 and modified by Senate Bill 113. Although carryover periods for credits with fixed expiration dates are tolled and extended by the number of taxable years a credit is disallowed under these caps, immediate cash-flow realization for high-income pass-through owners is capped at the lower of their Section 41(g) entity-attributable limit or $5,000,000. While SB 175 (R&TC §§ 17039.4 and 23036.4) introduced an irrevocable election on Form FTB 3870 (Election for Refundable Credit) allowing taxpayers to receive a 20% annual refundable payout over five years (beginning the third taxable year after the election year) for credits disallowed specifically by the $5,000,000 cap, the 2025 Form FTB 3523 instructions explicitly specify that S corporations cannot make this refundable election for entity-level credits, and credits restricted by general tax liability or the IRC § 41(g) pass-through limitation cannot be made refundable.

Furthermore, the 2025 FTB Form 3523 (Research Credit) instructions explicitly codify the Section 41(g) bar for disregarded business entities (single-member LLCs treated as sole proprietorships or corporate branches): a taxpayer owning an interest in a disregarded entity is limited to the difference between the regular tax computed with the income of the disregarded entity and the regular tax computed without the income of the disregarded entity, and if the single-member LLC reports a net tax loss for the year, the taxpayer is barred from claiming any credit from that disregarded entity in the current year and must carry the entire credit forward until the disregarded entity achieves profitability.
Judicial and Administrative Precedent Shaping Section 41(g) Enforcement

While federal appellate litigation turning solely on the arithmetic numerator of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) is relatively infrequent because the Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) fraction is mechanical, administrative and judicial rulings at both the state and federal levels establish the enforcement boundaries governing pass-through R&D credits.
California Office of Tax Appeals: Appeal of Walden et al. (2018-OTA-209)

In Appeal of Walden et al. (OTA Case Nos. 18010221, 18010222, and 18010223, 2018-OTA-209, decided November 28, 2018), the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) adjudicated a consolidated dispute involving California R&D tax credits claimed on amended returns for the 2003 through 2006 tax years ($54,543 for 2003; $55,458 for 2004; $89,784 for 2005; and $65,715 for 2006) by Walden Structures, Inc. (WSI), a California S corporation engaged in designing and constructing modular buildings, and passed through to its sole shareholder, Charles Walden. In framing the controlling legal architecture (specifically in Footnotes 5 and 6 of the opinion), the panel of administrative law judges explicitly confirmed the dual statutory interaction between R&TC § 23803 and IRC § 41(g): an S corporation is subject to California franchise and income tax at the 1.5% rate and is statutorily restricted under R&TC § 23803 to utilizing one-third (1/3) of its computed research credit against its entity-level franchise and income tax, whereas the S corporation's shareholders may utilize the passed-through research credits solely to offset personal income tax attributable to each shareholder's interest in the S corporation pursuant to IRC § 41(g).

Substantively, Walden centered on six agreed representative sample projects (Bramasole, Welk Resort, Mammoth Lakes Foundation Dorms, Mosque 1 & 2, Genentech, and Ynez Elementary) and examined whether WSI's modular design and engineering activities satisfied the four-part statutory test for qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1) (specifically technological uncertainty under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and the 80% "substantially all" process of experimentation requirement under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6)) and whether the activities fell within the statutory exclusions for the adaptation of an existing business component to a specific customer's requirement under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) or duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C). Applying Treasury Decision 9104 (T.D. 9104), the OTA held that the appellant met its burden of proof solely for the Mosque Project—which required extensive modeling and integration of novel structural features—while sustaining the FTB's disallowance for the remaining five sample projects. The OTA's decision underscores a crucial operational reality for pass-through owners: before the arithmetic limitation of Section 41(g) is ever reached on an individual return, the FTB conducts exhaustive, project-by-project substantiation audits at the entity level—often using statistical or judgmental project sampling—and any disallowance of underlying QREs cascades directly to eliminate both the 1/3 corporate offset and the 100% shareholder flow-through credit.
Passive Activity Collision: Garnett v. Commissioner (132 T.C. 368)

Even when a pass-through entity generates positive taxable income and satisfies the four-part test of IRC § 41(d), individual owners face a parallel statutory barrier under the passive activity loss and credit rules of IRC § 469. Under IRC § 469, if an individual owner does not "materially participate" in the pass-through entity's trade or business on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis, any passed-through R&D credit is classified as a passive activity credit and can only offset tax attributable to passive income. Consequently, an owner who fails material participation is caught in a dual statutory trap: the credit is simultaneously restricted by IRC § 469 (to passive tax liability) and by IRC § 41(g) (to the specific entity's tax liability).

Historically, the IRS exacerbated this trap for modern pass-through structures by asserting that all members of LLCs and partners in limited liability partnerships (LLPs) should be treated per se as "limited partners" under IRC § 469(h)(2) because their liability for entity debts is limited under state law to a determinable fixed amount under Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.469-5T(e)(3)(i)(B). Because limited partners under Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.469-5T(e)(2) are restricted to only three of the seven standard regulatory tests for material participation in Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.469-5T(a) (specifically tests (a)(1), (a)(5), and (a)(6)), the IRS position routinely trapped LLC and LLP losses and R&D credits as passive.

In the landmark decision Garnett v. Commissioner, 132 T.C. 368 (2009), involving taxpayers who held direct and indirect ownership interests in seven Iowa LLPs and two Iowa LLCs engaged in agribusiness operations, the United States Tax Court rejected the Commissioner's position. The Tax Court explained that Congress originally enacted IRC § 469(h)(2) because traditional state limited partnership statutes (such as the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 1916) prohibited limited partners from participating in business management without forfeiting their limited liability protection. Because LLP partners and LLC members are permitted under modern state law to participate actively in control and management without losing limited liability, the Tax Court held that their interests fit within the "general partner" exception of Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.469-5T(e)(3)(ii) and are not subject to the presumptive passive rule of IRC § 469(h)(2). Following Garnett and the parallel decisions in Thompson v. United States, 87 Fed. Cl. 728 (2009), and Newell v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2010-23, the IRS issued Action on Decision AOD 2010-02 (2010-14 I.R.B. 515, April 5, 2010, formally acquiescing in result only in Thompson) and promulgated proposed regulations published in the Federal Register on November 28, 2011, replacing the limited-liability standard with a management-rights test. Consequently, active managing members of R&D-performing LLCs and LLPs can establish material participation under any of the seven general tests of Temporary Treasury Regulation § 1.469-5T(a), neutralizing the passive activity credit bar and leaving 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) as the sole statutory ceiling governing credit absorption.
Regulatory Deference and Audit Strictness: Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner

The broader judicial posture toward R&D tax credit regulations further reinforces the necessity of adhering strictly to codified regulatory formulas such as Treasury Regulations §§ 1.41-7(c) and 1.53-3(c). In Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012) (Supreme Court Docket No. 12-684), the U.S. Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit examined whether raw hydrocarbon feedstock and production supplies consumed during full-scale commercial plant runs (testing an Amoco anti-coking compound in olefin cracking furnaces and a UCAT-J catalyst in polyethylene resin production) constituted qualified research supply expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1). The Second Circuit affirmed the disallowance of the normal production supply costs, relying first on the statutory structure of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) (which separates plant process research from the manufactured product) and second on administrative deference under Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452 (1997), to the Treasury Department's regulatory interpretation of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) excluding indirect research expenditures. This judicial scrutiny demonstrates that courts strictly enforce the text of IRC § 41 and formally promulgated Treasury Regulations—leaving pass-through taxpayers no viable legal basis to defend non-regulatory Section 41(g) calculation methods such as the marginal rate stack against the explicit fractional mandate of Treasury Regulations §§ 1.41-7(c) and 1.53-3(c) during an examination.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Step-by-Step Section 41(g) Computation

To demonstrate the exact arithmetic operation of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g), Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c), and R&TC §§ 23609 and 17052.12, consider a hypothetical compliance scenario involving a California resident individual filing as Single who holds a 50% managing member interest in a California engineering LLC taxed as a partnership. Under the precedent established in Garnett v. Commissioner, 132 T.C. 368 (2009), the managing member materially participates in the LLC's operations, thereby bypassing the passive activity credit restrictions of IRC § 469. During the taxable year, the engineering LLC incurs $100,000 in incremental California QREs over its base amount and computes a $15,000 net California R&D credit (at the 15% statutory rate under R&TC § 17052.12(b)(3)). Outside of the LLC, the taxpayer earns $200,000 in W-2 wage compensation from an unrelated corporate executive position.

In Scenario A (Profitable Entity), the LLC generates $100,000 of net ordinary business income; in accordance with IRC § 704(b) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(a)(3)(i), the taxpayer's Schedule K-1 (568) allocates $50,000 of ordinary business income and a $7,500 pass-through California R&D credit (50% share). Combining the $50,000 LLC income with the $200,000 W-2 wages yields an aggregate taxable income of $250,000 (ignoring personal deductions for simplicity) and an assumed pre-credit California income tax liability of $20,000, reflecting an 8% blended effective state tax rate. In Scenario B (Loss-Generating Entity), heavy R&D spending causes an operating deficit in which the LLC generates a -$50,000 net ordinary loss for the taxpayer on Schedule K-1 while still passing through the $7,500 R&D credit.

Analytical Synthesis and Technical Conclusions

A rigorous examination of 26 U.S.C. § 41(g) and its California counterparts under R&TC §§ 23609, 17052.12, and 23803 demonstrates that pass-through R&D tax credit realization is governed as much by entity-level taxable income modeling as by the technical substantiation of qualified research expenses. Because Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) ties the current-year credit ceiling strictly to the ratio of entity taxable income to total taxable income, pass-through structures operating in net loss positions experience immediate deferral of 100% of their flow-through R&D credits. While federal law provides a 1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward under IRC § 39 and California provides an indefinite carryforward under R&TC §§ 23609(f) and 17052.12(e), the statutory substitution rule ensures that these suspended credits can never be unlocked by unrelated wage, dividend, or capital gain income streams in future years.

Furthermore, the statutory election under IRC § 280C(c) between reducing IRC § 174A / § 174 deductions under § 280C(c)(1) and claiming a 79% reduced research credit under § 280C(c)(2) directly alters the entity's net ordinary income, thereby shifting the numerator of the Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3(c) fraction on every owner's individual tax return. Multi-year tax modeling must evaluate whether increasing entity taxable income via the standard § 280C(c)(1) deduction reduction yields a net tax savings after accounting for individual marginal tax rates, state conformity adjustments, and the resulting expansion of the Section 41(g) utilization ceiling. Finally, given the absence of regulatory authorization for the marginal rate stacking method for partnerships and S corporations under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-7(c), coupled with stringent IRS Appeals directives under IRM 8.7.1 and aggressive FTB audit enforcement exemplified in Appeal of Walden et al., pass-through entities and their owners must maintain contemporaneous substantiation of both project-level QREs under IRC § 41(d) and partner-level expenditure allocations under IRC § 704(b), while computing utilization ceilings strictly in accordance with the pro-rata fractional mandate of Treasury Regulation § 1.53-3.
